Notices of motion for the production of papers which the member asking for the same intends to move without discussion shall be marked by him with an asterisk and shall be placed by the clerk on the order paper above "Notices of Motions" under the heading "Notices of Motions for the Production of Papers." It seems to me the rule is very clear. Citation 436 under standing order 51 says:
Addresses are moved for papers and dispatches from the imperial government; for orders in council; for correspondence between the dominion, British and foreign governments, or between the dominion and provincial governments, or between the dominion and any company, corporation or individual.
It seems to me this clearly comes under that head. Paragraph 437 says:
The general rule is that information to be obtained from or through any of the revenue departments, any department under the treasury, or any department constituted or regulated by statute, is obtained by means of an order, whilst information to be obtained from or through a Secretary of State or the privy council is obtained by means of an address.
438. The information sought must relate to a matter of public importance and be obtainable through a public authority.
Surely there is no reason why this particular document should not be laid before the house. In any case on the point of order from which this discussion started I do not see that anything has occurred which gives it into the power of the minister to say that the moton should be transferred to another order.

subtopic: GRAIN HANDLING AT QUEBEC AND MONTREAL- REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS RESPECTING HANDLING, RATES AND ADMINISTRATION

I think if the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) would look into that phase of it he would be convinced-
Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East); That is another question.

subtopic: GRAIN HANDLING AT QUEBEC AND MONTREAL- REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS RESPECTING HANDLING, RATES AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Yes, it is another question. He would be convinced I think that it is a document that should be laid on the table. The general principle of the rule is stated very clearly, that if a public document is referred to by a minister it must be laid on the table in order that access may be had to it by all hon. members of the house so that they may be able to understand and appreciate its contents. The rule is based on sound public policy.
As far as the immediate motion is concerned, it seems to me it cannot be said to be in any sense a debatable motion, because the contents of the paper cannot be anticipated

Motions for Papers
in the discussion. The only question for debate is whether or not it is a public document, and inasmuch as it has been admitted that it is a document written by one of the members of what might be described as a governmental agency-that, it will be recalled, is the description given of it-surely it should now be produced. I am bound to say that I agree with what the right hon. gentleman has said as to the general question of debate, but this is not a debatable matter in the sense in which those words are used in our rules; because there it is, the contents are known, it is a specific document-specific, mark you. It is not as though this were a roving commission seeking to get something that is not known; there is the description of it: (a) the person who wrote it; (b) the person to whom it is written; (c) it clearly touches public business of, I think everyone will agree, the most outstanding kind, namely the question of rates.
I suggest to the minister, with great deference, that it might be well to let the order stand until it can be further looked into. If the Minister of Justice will examine the authorities with the care which he usually displays in matters of this kind I think he will conclude that having regard to all the circumstances this is not a debatable matter within the niles; and in any event the document should be laid on the table, having regard to the fact that the Minister of Transport referred to it in the terms in which he did the other day, and to the further fact that it is a specific document concerning which we have now the names of the addressee and the sender, and knowledge of the kind of public business to which it relates.

Before the house proceeds with the orders of the day I desire to direct attention to a matter which perhaps may be of more importance in the future than it is at the present time. On Friday last the right lion, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) moved:
That this house do now resolve itself into a committee to consider of a supply to be granted to His Majesty.
That motion was made in consequence of the committee having lapsed owing to there being no quorum on the preceding evening. Citation 47 under standing order 3 provides:
If the committee of supply, or ways and means, rises because there is not a quorum present, and therefore makes no report and does not ask leave to sit again, a motion with forty-eight hours' notice, unless unanimous consent is granted, must be made that the committee do sit again on some specified date.

speechtext: I was referring particularly to municipalities. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
That was true with
respect to the period since 1935 when the existing Dominion Housing Act was passed, for the reason that the definition of local housing authority is the same in this part

National Housing Act
of the new hill as it was in the old Dominion Housing Act, so that any amendment which might have been necessary to the municipal acts in the various provinces to enable municipalities to undertake housing schemes could, and in some cases may, have been made by provincial legislatures in the intervening period. I am not sure whether in a number of provinces at any rate specific amendment would be required to enable the municipality itself to undertake a housing scheme under this part, but certain it is that work that has been done-over seventeen million dollars worth of building that has been done under the existing Dominion Housing Act- has all been done by virtue of agreements between the Minister of Finance, as provided for in that act, and lending institutions. There is no case in the dominion where the municipality itself has taken advantage of that provision under the existing statute. It was thought wise, in carrying forward important parts of the existing statute into this bill, to leave the provision which would enable municipalities to assume the position of lending authority by agreement with the minister if they desired to do so and if, of course, as my hon. friend points out, they have authority so to do from the provincial legislatures. We cannot compel it but we can provide for them to act in that capacity provided they have both the legislative authority from the province and the desire to do it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: In order to clarify the situation it may be pointed out that there were several municipalities that did desire to take advantage of the housing act. The matter was placed before the union of municipalities and that body was asked to pass a resolution asking the provincial government to provide methods bjr which we could take advantage of the act. But it has not been done and therefore cannot be done until the next meeting of the provincial legislature in Victoria. That should be kpown and well known in order to avoid a lot of useless correspondence, because so far as British Columbia is concerned, the act cannot become operative until the next session of the legislature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
My hon. friend is going rather too far. The act can become operative, but the particular method of operating it by municipal action under this part cannot. He may be right in that, but certainly the other method provided by this part of the bill can continue as it is continuing at the present time to operate in British Columbia. I am pleased to be able to make this statement to the hon. member for New Westminster as
well as to other members from British Columbia, who have questioned me about the matter. I undertook some time ago to have the director of housing in the Department of Finance pay a visit to that province in an endeavour to find a means of meeting problems which have arisen there, and I have very encouraging reports from him as to the manner in which the provisions of the present housing act can be extended particularly to the interior of the province, from which locality there have come very many complaints of lack of facilities for obtaining loans under the act. I do not say that we can remove every difficulty. Of course, my hon. friend from Kootenay West is quite correct when he says that so far as the municipality acting is concerned, a change in provincial legislation in British Columbia will be necessary; but no municipality anywhere in the dominion has yet taken advantage of this particular feature of the present Dominion Housing Act. At the same time we felt it wise to retain the opportunity for them to do so if they received the necessary authority from the province and desired to take advantage of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
I do not recall lending institutions having indicated unwillingness to lend in certain parts of Canada particularly. In fact since I first had anything to do with the act we have endeavoured in every way to get lending institutions to make agreements with the dominion. It has been a slow process to persuade them to enter into agreements at all. I think I can say that it is only during the last year or year and a half we have had anything like the swing of progress in that direction which I should like to have seen. We have not attempted to dictate to lending institutions where they should lend. We have however endeavoured to persuade them to look for business in areas from which it was apparent, from correspondence coming to the department, that a demand existed from people who were able to give the necessary security and under conditions which would enable lending to be done with, in our opinion, reasonable certainty that the loan would be repaid. It will be seen however from my speech of last Wednesday, and from the contents of this bill as we proceed with it, that the great effort with respect to

part I is to overcome the deficiency which I pointed out on Wednesday last, that there are considerable areas in all provinces which up to now have not been able to get loans under the provisions of the housing act. When we come to section 4 we shall have opportunity of discussing the precise means by which we propose to overcome that situation. I think discussion on section 4 will clarify the intention in that regard.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
The minister said
these lending institutions were reluctant to enter into agreements. What reasons did they advance, or did they advance any reasons, for being reluctant?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: Not always the same. There is, to begin with, the general reluctance to enter into an entirely new method of doing business. That had to be overcome by a process of education as to what the Dominion Housing Act really meant from the standpoint of the lending institutions. And there are many institutions which do not particularly like the idea of being in partnership with the government. The process is one of educating the lending institutions in this method of cooperating with the government in meeting a problem. As to specific objections, there was the general question of the cost of operation. We were forcing quite a low rate of interest for the borrower from the standpoint of the lending institutions, and at the same time expecting them to make loans. The cost of making loans under the existing housing act, particularly in the smaller communities, averaged quite high. My hon. friend of course can understand that it is very much cheaper to make loans in a city where one man can inspect the construction of twenty or thirty houses at one time than it is in a community forty or fifty miles away from the company's office where only two or three or four loans are involved. That is a problem which we hope to solve by section 4 of the bill.

There is a very wide
distribution among small urban communites in Ontario, but not nearly so much so in other provinces. As to the province of Quebec, apart from the fifteen or sixteen municipalities which are comprised in the metropolitan area of Montreal there are about a dozen communities in which loans have been made; but Quebec is one of the provinces from which complaints have come. For instance, there is the Gaspe peninsula. It can be readily understood that while there are a number of thriving small communities on the Gaspe peninsula, it is difficult to get the lending institutions to undertake the expense of making loans, taking care of the cost of inspection during construction, and so on. That is one of the areas I have in mind that may be helped by section 4 of the bill. In New Brunswick there are about a dozen districts in which loans have been made. In Nova Scotia I should say there were about fifteen communities. In Prince Edward Island there is only one, Charlottetown. In Manitoba, apart from the district that might be called the Winnipeg metropolitan area, there are only three places in which loans have been made. My hon. friend from Regina was not quite correct with regard to Saskatchewan; one loan is in Prince Albert and one is in Yorkton. In British Columbia, if we exclude the Vancouver metropolitan area, there are only nine municipalities in which loans actually had been made up to the end of May last.

speechtext: That is in municipalities, but I think my hon. friend was inquiring more about rural districts. The minister used the word "urban". That indicates an organized district, but I should like to know if any loans have been made in rural communities not big enough to be towns or villages, just settlements of five or six hundred people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
Frequent reference is
made here in this list of areas in which loans have been made to townships, but of course I must make it clear that this is not a farm
loan act. Under this bill, it is not possible to make loans on farms. The loans are on the homes, and as a practical question one can see immediately how difficult it would be to have a separate mortgage on a farm house with the farm under a farm mortgage. It was never contemplated by the authors of the original bill, I am sure, that it should meet that situation. But there is no reason why, with the changes we are proposing in section 4-and you are still compelling me to discuss that section before we reach it- the object of the bill should not be attained, which is to widen the application of the principles of the housing act in its relationship to communities which are not now being served by it, no matter what their class may be; but of course I cannot pretend that it is a farm loan act. We have a farm loan act on the statute books, and we have a farm loan board operating. Under this bill we cannot make loans on farms, but the lending institutions can make loans on rural homes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES

speechtext: The view expressed by my right hon. friend is that the words should be "connected with any loan," and we are proposing to make it "necessary to complete the house." That is a minor amendment, but it has arisen out of the experience the legal officers have had with odd, peculiar cases. That is all.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: That is what I had in mind. Should we pay legal expenses for the purpose of completing the house, where it may involve litigation in no sense related to the loan, but which must be disposed of before the loan can be made? I have particular cases which have arisen in which litigation was pending. A man wants a loan, and he gets that litigation wound up and acquires title. In doing so he spends $150 or $200. As this reads now it is broad enough to include that amount in the cost of the house, and in my judgment it has no relation to such cost. I think there was some discussion along that line either in this house or out of it. National Housing Act

of investigation. I can conceive of others where a community will desire to do something in the way of a community effort in the development of a particular area. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

One of the reasons for bringing down legislation of this kind is that we all know that people have not been building as many houses as they should have. This whole bill is designed to facilitate the building of more houses because of the opinion we all have that Canada and the people of Canada need houses to a greater extent than they have been provided in the last few years.
I would not undertake to send out an investigator to find out why people did not build houses. I would much prefer to bring down legislation such as this, which is intended to help them build more houses, because the reasons why they have not done so during the last number of years would range over a very wide variety of opinions. One man's opinion would be one thing, another man's opinion would be another, and the reasons would differ in various parts of Canada. So I doubt if any practical good would come of appointing people to find out why houses have not been built in sufficient numbers. I should prefer to proceed on the constructive lines which this bill contemplates of making it easier for houses to be built in the future.

speechtext: I have listened to speeches loud, long and emphatic on this side of the house pointing out why the government should embark upon a cheap housing or rental scheme, and I was enthusiastically behind those speakers, because that is one of the needs of the time. Before section 3 passes I wish to say I looked through the bill and failed to find any other section dealing with investigations and complaints. Reading paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e), we find that practically all these provisions have already under the act been carried out, but I should like to ask the minister what form of investigation he proposes in regard to the actual construction of the homes after the work is started. I have in mind a recent investigation in Halifax county, particularly in connection with the town of Dartmouth,

when there were two groups of houses constructed, one a group of twenty and the other a group of ten. The construction was faulty. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES

There is a limit to the extent to which the government can wet-nurse both the lending institutions and the man borrowing money for the construction of a house in which he is to live. As a matter of fact there are three parties, because the contractor enters into the matter. With respect to the Halifax incident, because of noise made locally, I felt it desirable to send the director of housing to see what exactly the condition was, and in that connection I have a report indicating that the matters referred to were very much exaggerated. The lending institution and the owner are both interested in seeing that the house is built according to the specifications, and they are there right on the ground watching their own interests. Why call upon the dominion government to step in between two parties who have a definite contract, the specifications of which have been approved under the dominion housing scheme? We simply cannot undertake as a government to

National Housing Act
wet-nurse the parties to these contracts, I put it bluntly. Surely they are capable of looking after their own interests in a reasonable way. The owner of the house is interested in seeing that the contractor carries out his contract; the lending institution, which is risking sixty per cent of the money, is interested in seeing that a good job is done. The government has taken an interest in the matter to ensure that the specifications on which 'the house is to be built, the specifications included in the contract, shall be those of a reasonably well constructed house of the type desired, but it seems to me that is as far as the government should be expected to go. After that, the interests of the various parties ought to ensure that the house is built as it should be. I believe there was some deficiency but not nearly the deficiency that the reports indicate. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
My hon. friend mixes
up two things when he speaks in terms of money. The provision in this part of the bill is clear, as will be seen a little later; it is $20,000,000 as far as governmental expenditure is concerned under this part. One may estimate what the total amount of building made possible by the dominion putting in $20,000,000 will be; that is a matter of estimate. Under the existing act the dominion has invested up to the present about

$4,500,000, if my memory is correct, and $17,000,000 of building has resulted. If we apply the same proportions to the $20,000,000 authorized by this part of the bill, it would give somewhere in the neighbourhood of $80,000,000. Then in part II provision is made for $30,000,000 to be advanced by the dominion for low rental housing schemes. In connection with that, either ten per cent in the case of a municipality undertaking the scheme or twenty per cent in the case of a limited dividend housing corporation must be added to what the dominion puts in. Under the third part of the bill we make a taxation subsidy. If you add the whole thing together you might get $100,000,000, you might get $120,000,000. The bill is intended to stimulate the investment of capital by the man who wants to own a home and by the institution which has money seeking an outlet but which is afraid of the risk; and part III is to help for a period of years in connection with the taxation on new low cost homes. That is the whole principle of the measure. I did not intend by this legislation to bring in the millennium, but it represents a carefully thought out means of assistance in connection with what we all recognize to be a serious problem; one in connection with which, as I said 'the other day, we have only limited jurisdiction; we can assist only financially, and some eminent authorities even question our authority to do that. It is intended as an attack upon this particular problem, not as a means of bringing about a new heaven and a new earth.

National Housing Act

our industries, the one most laggard in advancing, in taking advantage of possibilities of improved technique, of lowering costs, of the standardizing of commodities, is the building industry. With respect to investigations, the laws of Canada provide through the combines act and other legislation means of dealing with some of the matters to which my hon. friend refers. speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
Perhaps we might pass the first item, branch administration, dealing with expenditures in connection with the head office of the Indian Affairs branch. Remarks on the potlatch might better come under item No. 163. However, it is immaterial.
Supply-Indian Affairs

The whole administration of the Indian Affairs department must necessarily have undergone some change by reason of the consolidation of departments, and as this is the first opportunity the minister has had to explain what changes have been brought about in the administration, and this being the administration item, he might be able to make a short statement as to what is now the administrative practice with respect to Indians as covered by this item.

Very few changes have taken place in the administration since the consolidation of these various departments under mines and resources; that is, if the question of the leader of the opposition has reference to organic changes in administration. Previously the Indian Affairs department was a separate department of government; I believe it was associated with the Department of the Interior, under one minister.
And he was Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

The Superintendent General was the Minister of the Interior of the day. There was a deputy superintendent general, who under the set-up of the new department becomes director of Indian administration. The work of the Indian Affairs department continues as it has been hitherto, prior to the union of the various departments into the Department of Mines and Resources. It is concerned with education, medical care, welfare work, administration of agencies all over Canada and the like. We are endeavouring to make some changes in the administration, not in the organic sense, but more in the direction in which the work relating to this very important department is carried on.
In my opinion, Indian Affairs administration is one of the problems of this country. There was a time, if we look back thirty-five or forty years, or to more distant periods, when the consensus of opinion throughout Canada was that the Indian problem, if we had an Indian problem, would probably solve itself with the effluxion of time. At that time there was a decline year by year in the Indian population of Canada. That has changed now and our Indian population is on the increase, increasing at the rate of about one and one-half per cent per annum. That is due to better care. If we compare the expenditures in medical services alone at the present time with what they were thirty-five or forty years ago, we see that there has been a vast increase in the amounts of money voted by parliament each year for medical care, hospitalization, and general welfare work. All this has tended naturally, as it was intended to do,

to lift the standard of living of the Indians. Better medical care and better hospitalization mean lower mortality, and they are the factors which I think may be said to be mainly responsible for the change-over from a declining to an increasing Indian population.
For instance, in these estimates we have included $275,000 looking towards the eradication of tuberculosis in our Indian population. Tuberculosis has been one of the most difficult diseases to combat among the Indians, and we find that as our various provincial administrations have taken steps to deal with it in the white population it is necessary to deal with it among the Indians. As I intimated to the committee a year ago, representations have been made from practically every province urging the federal government to take some steps to reduce and control mortality from tuberculosis among the Indians. Every reserve was a centre of infection, and consequently pressure of public opinion in that direction has moved on further towards inducing the federal administration to take some preliminary steps this year in a program looking to that end.

Oh, it has been going
on for years.
Not directly with tuberculosis.
Oh, yes.
Well, we shall not quarrel over that.

No; I am only glad it
is so.

The point I want to make is that the effect of all this is simply to decrease the mortality and accelerate the increase in Indian population.
We have another problem, in this sense, that practically one-third of the Indian population of Canada are known as hunting and trapping Indians; that is, Indians who live by the chase. They are mostly in the northern parts of our provinces. The reserves where they are located are not suitable for agriculture. They live by fishing as far as their food supplies are concerned, and by the chase and such purchases of other food as they may be able to make from their meagre income.
Some of them get treaty money.

The treaty money is a
comparatively small item. No one can say that the treaty money was a generous provision for the Indians; it was not. But the effect of all this is being seen more clearly

Supply-Indian Affairs
as the years pass. Since the resources were turned over to the western provinces there has been a marked increase in the number of white trappers trapping in these areas where formerly the Indian had free sway. Owing, I think, to rather short-sighted policies which governments of Canada have at times followed, there has been a decline, and in some places almost complete eradication, of the fur-bearing animals. As the number of fur-bearing animals went down, the natural means of livelihood of the Indians went down also, and they were thrown in greater degree from year to year into dependence upon the federal administration. That, to my mind, is one of the serious problems we are facing in respect to at least one-third of the Indian population of this country. It is estimated that the Indian population to-day is about 118,000, and at the present rate of increase it will not be many years before it reaches 150,000. If some steps cannot be taken to enable our Indian population to depend more upon their own resources, it is a safe assumption that they will become an increasing burden upon the state. To-day many of these Indians desire to become more or less independent. That was one of the reasons behind the legislation I introduced a few weeks ago to set up a revolving fund from which advances might be made to individual Indians, or to Indians on reserves in a communal sense, or to Indian schools, for the purpose of providing materials to educate Indian girls and boys in handicraft arts.
Would it interrupt the minister to ask the relative number of the 118,000 in the east and the west?
British Columbia has about 24,000.
That is, who live by the chase and fishing?
Well, some live by fishing; some work in the lumber or logging camps.
And canneries.

But in the main they live by the chase. Alberta has about 11,000; Saskatchewan, 12,000; Manitoba, 13,000; Ontario, about 30,000; Quebec, 13,000, and there are about 4,000 altogether in the maritime provinces and the remainder in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. That is a rough approximation of the distribution of the Indian population.
Of that type, or of the whole?
The whole population.
The minister said one-third of the Indians lived by hunting and fishing, and then he said that number was 118,000.

No; the total number is about 118,000; roughly one-third of those are regarded as hunting and trapping Indians, or something under 40,000.
Many of the reserves are suitable for agriculture, and efforts are being made on those reserves to induce the Indians to take up that mode of livelihood. In Ontario many of them find opportunities for work, some of them adjacent to mining camps, others in the pulpwood industry and the like. I recall a few reserves east of Port Arthur where this work has been taken up; contracts were made for the delivery of pulpwood; they also engage in the manufacture of canoes, snowshoes, skis, and I believe they have taken some contracts for supplying grain doors for railway cars and that sort of thing.
The problem is an interesting one, and difficult in some aspects. It must be borne in mind that since the beginning of Indian administration they have been regarded as wards of the state. Under the terms of the surrenders of their lands there is a definite responsibility in wardship on the part of the federal government to the Indians. But I think the methods we have followed in the past have tended to perpetuate that idea among the Indians themselves. I recognize the difficulty of changing that state of affairs. I am not optimistic enough to think that change will be other than gradual and slow. But I do think we can shape the policy of Indian administration to that end, not only in the administration of the reserves, but as well in the whole field of Indian education.
I wish to pay tribute to the splendid work done by the various churches in the field of Indian education. I know I shall not be misunderstood if I say that I think there were times when a somewhat different direction might have been given to education and much better results thereby secured. If mistakes have been made in the past in that respect, it has been in the effort to graft.the white man's way too quickly upon the Indian population. I know of Indian girls and boys coming to the residential schools at the age of six or seven, remaining perhaps ten or twelve years, acquiring an education in the sense we ordinarily understand, the ability to read and write and figure, the three R's, learning habits of personal cleanliness, how to operate an electric washing machine and an electric iron; but when they left the school there was only one place for them to go, namely,

Supply-Indian Affairs
back to the reserve, and often the education they received in the schools was not adapted to that mode of living. I may say that I have discussed this matter with many of those engaged in educational work in connection with the churches, and I have found nothing but the finest spirit of cooperation when I offered some suggestion as to where I thought improvements might be made in that respect. I think the education could be made more vocational in character,, with much better results.
So far as the organic set-up of the branch is concerned, those members of the committee who are interested will find the details on page 188 and succeeding pages in the report of the Department of Mines and Resources, tabled at the beginning of this session, for the year ending March 31, 1937. Generally speaking, there are five divisions in the branch, with some subdivisions. First, there is the division of field administration, which has to do with supervision of the various Indian reserves and agencies throughout Canada. Second, there is the medical service, which has grown to very considerable proportions. There is next a division that has to do with reserves and trusts. For instance, there is something between thirteen and fourteen million dollars of trust funds, or band funds as we call them, in the branch. Some of the bands have very large funds. The greater number, however, have very little if any; probably a majority of the reserves have no band funds at all. The next division is the welfare and training service, which has to do with the educational side of the activities of the department and the general welfare work. Then there is a records service, where all the records of the administration are kept and classified, so that information going back as long as there has been an administration may be available.
That very briefly sets out the five general divisions into which the Indian administration work is divided. Possibly this brief summary, given in a rather fragmentary fashion, will give members of the committee an idea of the general set-up, and I shall be glad to supply any additional information when we discuss the items in detail.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the members of the committee appreciate, as I do, what the minister has said. I confess that to me the Indian problem has always been one of great interest and, I might add, of considerable concern. I know that the changes which have been made during the last ten years have been marked and very striking indeed. We have provided for the care of the Indians in this country a medical service

which in my judgment is as good as that of any country in the world, if not better. It has involved the expenditure of substantial sums of money, but I think the reasons given by the minister as to why we should deal with tuberculosis and other diseases in the manner in which we are endeavouring to deal with them need not be amplified by me.
There are essentially two problems of which we have to think in connection with the Indian. The one concerns his living, which is very important, and the other concerns his health, which may be divided into his mental and physical health and his spiritual wellbeing. The churches are not lacking in their efforts to care for the latter; and upon us rests the responsibility for caring for his body and mind, and in a broad and general way I think we have made great advances in that regard. The minister has detailed them. I need not go into them now, because there are some about which I may have to offer some little criticism as we proceed. As to his getting a living, after all the Indian regards that as important, and in my observation he is not alone in that regard. How is he to get a living? At some points in the east they have splendid reserves. They farm; they are agriculturists in the large sense of the term, and they do very well. In some of the western reserves, for instance at the Blackfoot reserve at Gleichen, they have their coal mines and their cattle on the ranges, and grain is grown in considerable quantities. You have the cattle ranges of the Indians at Macleod and in that section of the country; and then you have the Stoneys who are essentially hunters. On the rocky reserve which they inhabit the Stoneys are unable to make for themselves an adequate living. So you have two classes to consider when you come to the question of a living: one class that lives by its hunting and fishing ability, on the' proceeds of the chase-and each year it is getting more difficult, as the minister has pointed out, to make a living in that way-and the other class.
How are you going to care for the first class? That	is	a real	problem. There areforty thousand people who must be cared for. We exercise supervision over them. We have given them reserves, and they have surrendered their rights	to	surrounding territory.	Thereserves are not sufficient, either in area or in quality of soil, to produce a living. That problem we	have not	mastered. We	haveplayed with	it,	and I	do not mean	that
offensively. We have attempted to deal with that branch of it, but we have had no settled policy to deal with it, and I do not know what policy we could adopt. You could not

I think the effort to stimulate the activity of the individual Indians, as indicated by the bill passed the other day. by means of the revolving fund, may have some beneficial results; but, Mr. Chairman, the Indian is still an Indian. He cannot change his racial characteristics, which are as firm and as well marked to-day as they were when this country was discovered. They have been weakened by contact with the whites; they have suffered the consequences of contagious diseases which they have contracted; they have been weakened physically; but essentially the Indian is still an Indian.
I am going to say something that may be regarded as almost heresy, but I do not think the efforts we are making to educate the Indians are worth any fraction of the money we spend in doing so. This is not a sudden conversion; I have had this conviction for many years. I have looked into the matter pretty closely, and frankly I do not think we are getting from our endeavours to educate the Indians results that are at all comparable with the results that might be obtained by the expenditure of the same money in endeavouring to make the Indian economically independent. I believe that a limited expenditure of money towards education, and generous expenditures towards developing his tendency to improve his own position economically will give us excellent results.
I happen to know of three or four cases which came to my direct attention. As the minister stated, we take ten or twelve years to educate a boy or a girl. I have in mind a boy-I believe the minister spoke about a girl -who six months after the time he was out of school was back to the reserve, the only place where he could go. I am sorry to say that boy was just plain ignorant. What is more, Mr. Chairman-and I regret to say thisfrom the standpoint of his tribe and his contribution to the life of his band, he is not as good as was his contemporary who did not go to school at all; for it has unfitted him,
unless he drops straight down into the stratum from which he came.
There is the difficulty. I know the minister is deeply interested in the matter. I confess one never talks to an Indian of intelligence without looking at him and wondering what is in the back of his head; for he has a tradition; he has an uncanny way of knowing things. He has a knowledge of everything about him which makes him one of the most wonderful studies to be found in this world. He looks out across the great prairie and you see in his eye something more than the mere looking at the land, the trees, the forests or the mines. You see something which makes you realize that he is thinking of days and generations which have gone by, when he had handed down to him from sire to son, and on and on and on, the story of their past. If you could only get them to tell you about it, you would realize how difficult is the problem to make of them something they are not. All you have to do is to visit the burial ground of the Blackfoot tribe and see where their old leader was laid away, and the provision they made for his future. You see how he was to go to the Happy Hunting Ground, and the way in which he was to carry on when he got there. You see the provisions that those who had been left behind made for him as he went, the little covering they placed over the supplies which were to serve him in that Happy Hunting Ground. You need only to see these things to realize how difficult is the problem of dealing with them.
I assure the minister that any assistance which can be given to improve their physical condition, their health, their happiness of mind, or anything which bears directly on their happiness of mind or on efforts to strengthen their physical resistance to the very conditions to which the minister referred, is time well spent. Speaking as a Canadian I am extremely proud of the way in which we have handled our Indians. True, at times we have made mistakes; but in the main we have treated them better than have most countries. If we have deprived them of their inheritance, we have at least paid a price for it, and we shall continue to do so till the end.

I do not refer to the savagery of old times, but to the refined type of savagery which has developed from their contact with the white man, which has come about as a result of our having appropriated their property, and given them reserves.

What is the use in sending these Indian children to school to teach them modern civilization and then having them come home to something like that? We should give some consideration to the homes of these Indians as well as to providing schools on the reservation. I saw many of the children attending these schools and they appeared just as bright as other children, but they seemed to lose their brightness once they left school. I found the officials to be very good. The doctors, the Indian agents and the police officers were a fine type of men. I found the teachers in the school on the reservation to which I refer to be excellent. The doctor on one reservation discussed the matter of tuberculosis with me. He suggested that on those reservations where there are no hospitals, hospitals should be provided. The Indian parents love their children just as much as other parents, and they do not want to have them sent to hospitals many miles away from the reservation. In order to prevent this, they try to hide the fact that their children have tuberculosis. This doctor told me that if I lifted my voice at all in this connection, I should try to persuade the minister and the department to establish hospitals on those reservations where there is none. Unfortunately that is something we cannot control. The Indians in northern Ontario, and indeed in several provinces, are now segregated almost entirely upon reserves. I found this to be one great difficulty, that they did not know whether they had a credit or a debit, what was coming to the tribe or what was in trust for the tribe and whether they could or could not use it. They were absolutely in the dark. I talked with two of the chiefs and some of the young men who have been through the schools and are fluent, bright young fellows.

In addition to other things, they feel that they should be consulted more than they are in connection with what is planned for them. On the reserves I visited I had some conversation with the farm instructors and also with the Indians. In one instance I found that the stock was greatly depleted. I asked the instructor how long he had been there and he said, "Some twenty odd years." I asked what was the amount of stock on the reserve when he went there, and he told me. I asked what the stock amounted to then at the time of my visit, and found it was less than half what it had been in the first place. As a consequence the Indians are putting up hay, getting a permit, peddling a load now and then, and doing the same with firewood and things of that kind. I should like the minister, if he would, to explain the system and show how the Indians stand with the department at Ottawa, and how they may get an accounting of the funds held in trust for them.

I am dealing with the point raised in regard to the Indians getting information as to the position of their band funds. The chief and counsellors of the tribe can always get that information from the Indian agent. If he has not that information he can easily obtain it, and there is no reason why it should not be given to the Indians. As a matter of fact I think we have the right to use the increment of the fund for the purposes of the Indians without

their consent, in connection with certain matters such, as relief and medical care, but no disposition can be made of band funds without the approval of the Indians themselves. On the other hand the Indians cannot dispose of the band funds without the approval of the administration. In other words, before band funds can be utilized for any purpose both the Indians who are interested in the fund and the department which administers it must agree as to its disposition. As I have already said, so far as I know there is no reason why the chief and his counsellors should not be able to ascertain at any time the standing of their fund and the disposition that has been made of it.
With reference to the other point, of course I do not know the reserve to which my hon. friend refers. I think what he has stated is true on some reserves; that is, that if anything they have progressed backward in their agricultural methods in the last twenty or twenty-five years. That is due perhaps to, shall I say, indifference in administration; or perhaps a farm instructor gets into a rut, as human beings sometimes do, and does not take his job seriously enough. The check on that I think is better and more constant supervision. I am bound to say this, that I think in the past administrations have perhaps erred on the side of too much economy in the administration of these services. If I could induce my colleagues to expand the Indian vote, I think I see where I could spend another $100,000 to excellent advantage. But even without that I hope a steady improvement will take place.
I wish, however, to say this to the committee. I do not think there is any more important unit in the administration than the man who has charge of the reserve, the farming instructor on the reserve, and those who have to do with the Indians in their day to day contacts. If there is understanding, sympathy, firmness and intelligence in dealing with situations as they arise, unquestionably you get better results. On the other hand if, as unfortunately may be the case in some instances, officials lack those qualities, then you have a certain amount of suspicion, distrust and retrogression. Probably that is the situation in the reserve to which my hon. friend refers.

I am very happy to hear that expression of opinion on the part of the minister, but I am given to understand that the agent will not give the chief or his counsellors information as to how the band stands with the department at Ottawa. Supposing they have a credit which they wish to invest

The circumstances of each individual case will be studied. If you have a reserve that is adapted to the rearing of cattle,
I would hope that we would be able to put some stock, at any rate, on that reserve, and see that hay was put up to feed the animals and that they were properly looked after. If the venture were properly handled there would be a natural increase, and there is no reason on earth why on a reserve that is adapted to stock raising there should not be a substantial herd of cattle. In some instances some of these animals may be owned by individual Indians; or it may be a communal effort on the part of the band, but again I stress the importance of supervision and care in dealing with these questions. Sometimes, by his traditional way of living, the Indian becomes careless in looking after stock, and it is necessary to have someone to see that the stock is properly cared for. That is all part of the whole scheme of general welfare and improvement among these Indians. I know it is going to be a long, patient business, but I do think it offers some possibilities of getting many of these people into a much better position than they are in to-day. At any rate that is the principle which is guiding us in this action.

I should like to express to the minister my appreciation for the vision which he manifested in his speech regarding the development of fur farming and other activities among the Indians. It is my feeling that he is producing very fine results, and I should like to encourage him. I believe he certainly should have that other $100,000 because beyond question there is arising among the Indians a very definite need. May I use as an illustration the reserve in my own constituency. For a long time the Indians have been able to go off the reserve and work at such jobs as picking up potatoes, harvesting beets, and working in the grain fields. The returns from that kind of labour supplemented their regular income. However, since the coming of the depression it has been virtually impossible for the Indian to get any such work, with the result that many of them
are suffering painfully. Unless something is done on the reserve to replace the revenue they have lost through their inability to get employment, manifestly the Indians are going to tend to decay in numbers and morale.
I believe the minister is thoroughly justified in asking for sufficient money to develop industries on the reserve. He has mentioned fur farming and stock raising as being possibilities. The reserve in my constituency would be well adapted to stock raising and also to grain growing. A good deal of the ground has been ploughed up, and in many instanses grain has been grown. In some respects, however, some of the Indians do not find themselves adapted to farming, though others do it very well. A number of them have found that the grasslands from which they cut their hay have been depleted, and for that reason they have been placed in a difficult position. If money were available and if the Indians who were adapted to fur farming were encouraged to go into it, it would be a great blessing.
I greatly appreciate what the minister has said, and I for one will certainly support him in any requests for additional money he may make to help the Indian. I believe the Indians are a very important element of our growing population.
Is there any coordination between the minister's department and the tourist bureaux? I refer particularly to the contact with guides.

Yes; we are trying an experiment this year, which will probably answer the hon. member's question. We are taking over some bright boys who have been recommended to us by the principals in Indian schools. They are to be given training to act as guides in our parks, under the supervision of experienced park wardens. If the experiment works out satisfactorily, we shall expand the effort. This plan -may give opportunities to a number of these lads to become engaged in useful occupation.
I have suggested to some who are in Charge of the more northern schools that the boys be given some training in the art of guiding-because I am told it is an art-so that on occasions they may find useful work. So far as the matter of correlation with the tourist industry is concerned, I am not just sure what the hon. member had in mind, but I believe it is possible to link up the production of handicraft work among the Indians with a sales system for the benefit of United States or English tourists who may come to Canada. There is one phase of the Indian question to which I should like to refer for a moment, and when I have concluded I should like to hear the minister's observations on the matter. In southern British Columbia we find a considerable number of reserves. In my own constituency they are dotted all the way down the valley of the Similkameen river, and through the Okanagan valley. There is no doubt that in times past the Okanagan band must have covered a very considerable part of what is now the state of Washington, and have reached well into the present province of British Columbia. The difficulty to which I allude is that by intermarriage and constant visiting a mix-up has developed between United States and Canadian Indians. At times there is evidence of unrest, and when the trouble is looked into it generally boils down to a question of jealousy between United States and Canadian Indians. I often wonder whether this difficulty is confined to this particular part of British Columbia. It does not seem to me to be reasonable that there should be Indians of the same tribe resident on reserves in the state of Washington who are receiving certain benefits from Canada, while there are Indians resident on our reserves who are receiving official assistance from the United States government. I wonder if it would not be possible to arrive at some solution of this problem so that there might be a definite understanding between the two governments, or at least between the two departments of government that administer the matter? Perhaps a separation could take place between the Indians who are definitely Canadian and those who are definitely United States. If this were not a cause of friction, there would be no reason to raise the question, but I am persuaded that it is. I have had it up with the minister and with the deputy superintendent, and I should like the minister to let us have his observations.

The only places where the difficulty referred to by the hon. member is to be found is on the Okanagan reserve in British Columbia, and in Manitoba, perhaps to a lesser degree, in connection with the Sioux Indians. As my hon. friend says, there

I desire to compliment the minister and the committee upon the sympathetic attitude displayed toward these original Canadians. They are obviously permanently among us, and our duty is to improve their circumstances in every way possible and to do everything reasonable in providing education. We should try to attract these people to the soil because they make splendid farmers. A large number of ploughing matches are held throughout Ontario every fall. For some years it was necessary to have the Indians in separate classes at these matches, but more recently they have resented this and have asked that they be placed in the same classes with the white men. In many instances they have carried off the championships. I believe there should be strong supervision, both temporal and spiritual, on these reserves. This is the duty that we should accept as a matter of course, since they are wards of the government.

I listened to the minister with some degree of interest when he referred to the educational policy being pursued by the government. It naturally gladdens the heart of an educationalist to hear that modem methods are creeping into the administration of the schools on the Indian reserves. I am hoping that the minister will persevere along this line so that the Indians may have the benefit of modem improvements.
Has the minister any further information as to the condition now prevailing on the branch reserve at Oka? I understand this is a branch of the Caughnawaga reserve. I have taken up this matter with the department, and I am interested to know whether there are any further developments and a possibility of a permanent solution of this problem.

The Indians at Oka have not title to the lands upon which they are
living. This story goes back into ancient history. The order of Sulpicians was given a grant over two hundred years ago to land in this particular district, and my information is that at that time the Indians were allowed to stay. Some question has arisen in more recent years as to their right to be there, and this has given rise to some local difficulty.
If I remember rightly, they claim title by prescription.
I am advised that a case was carried to the privy council, and the ruling was against the Indians staying there.
I knew of their claim, but I had forgotten about the decision.

It is a difficult problem, and I may say to the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) that it has engaged the attention of the department for some time past. I am not prepared at the moment to say just what will be the final solution, but it is a rather knotty problem.

I understand the land has been sold by the Sulpician order to a Belgian concern, and the Indians have lost their rights to the woodland. At the present time I think the department have to purchase the wood and deliver it to the Indian reserve. Of course, the Indian still desires to go into the same bush he and his ancestors have been going into for some two hundreds years, and they are constantly being arrested for trespassing. It is giving rise to a certain amount of discontent among the Indians and considerable apprehension among the whites living in the immediate vicinity. I took the matter up with the department and received every consideration. I know the department is anxious to find a reasonable solution, and I was wondering if we had come any nearer to a solution or if the plan might be to move these Indians to a more desirable place, perhaps even to some other province, where they might be located to better advantage. I know the Indians would be loath to leave that particular spot which they have inhabited for several hundred years. Their old burying ground is there, and naturally they have an attachment to that particular part of Canada and feel that they have been deprived of their rights; but with a little gentle persuasion from the department, the Indians, if they were tactfully handled, could, I believe, be induced to move to a more desirable place where they would enjoy more freedom than they are enjoying to-day.

Mr. Chairman, I feel constrained to impose somewhat on the time of the committee to deal at some length with the custom of the potlatch among the Indians of British Columbia, and especially those Indians of the Kwawkewlth agency, of which the head and front might be said to be Alert Bay. In the session of 1936 the government introduced an amendment to the Indian Act designed to establish greater strictures against this custom of the potlatch; but owing almost entirely to the efforts of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), the member for the district in which this agency lies, the minister withdrew his amendment, and the act remains in statu quo ante. In that controversy I had myself taken some part, and predisposed thereto by a principle I have long held, supported the hon. member in his contentions. This principle was that customs of native peoples in contact with the culture of the present day, or the culture of any day for that matter, tended to sublime and the bad features of the custom to fall away and become only an interesting memory.
However, the situation in one part of British Columbia is quite different. About a year after the above discussion took place I received a very earnest communication from the Reverend F. Comley of Oak Bay, near Victoria, pleading for my cooperation, and to 
this letter I replied immediately stating that, if possible, at a later date I would investigate the condition nearer to its happening. In the meantime I developed considerable correspondence in an effort to discover whether there was a real grievance in and around the agency. I could read here copious extracts from this correspondence and detail much of the information I have received; but I am disposed to be very much the other way in the general objection to the potlatch which many of my correspondents voice, because it has always been my impression that the wisdom of the real conqueror, of the real colonist, of the real leader of people, is best demonstrated when he permits his conquered people or those over whom he exercises dominion to retain their customs and tribal traditions.
In this Kwawkewlth agency, however, I believe we are definitely facing a traditional rite and custom from which some of the bestializing elements have not been sufficiently or speedily enough removed, and it appears to me to be our duty to listen to the protests that are being made, to discover the reason and to remedy the cause.
My own inquiries made in Alert Bay and elsewhere from both potlatch Indians and those who have already renounced the potlatch leave me only with this conclusion:	It
is admittedly very difficult to understand the genesis of the potlatch; but if one goes outside the Indians ample evidence throughout history abounds of emissaries from one nation visiting a strange or neighbour nation bearing gifts to the potentate, arranging peace pacts, and returning to their own ruler with the largess of the country they have visited. The Arabian Nights, that cradle of our romantic literature, abounds in just such stories. Holy Writ has also complete evidence of the fact that these things had existed from ancient times. It is extremely likely that along the coast of British Columbia, with its many islands, there were in former times many self-contained tribes or phratries of Indians of widely differing origins just as there are to-day, and that because they could not read or write or count or estimate, it became necessary for them to rely upon memory for such records of history as, for instance, the marriage of the scion of one tribe into another or any other historical circumstance, which the tribe wished to record and remember. The ceremony of marriage, birth or death must under such circumstances be observed by the largest possible number of people even if they had to be brought from far cape Flattery in the south or from Fort Simpson in the far north. Such a gathering,

Supply-Indian Affairs
invested with all the traditions of'the people, was coloured by dancing and made festive and notable by gifts.
Undoubtedly it formed in the history of these primitive peoples a definite encouragement to peace and promoted a union of interest as frequently as it did also union of blood. In the primitive lives of these people, living on the bountiful products of nature, gifts were simple in themselves or at the most they represented the deft workmanship of the worker, either weaver or carver, or some other clever or deft workman and were unique and valuable for that reason. There is great difficulty-and I have asked many questions about it-in discovering the origin of the word "potlatch," but it does appear to have come out of the Chinook jargon and to be definitely related to the giving of gifts. The giving of these gifts has always taken place at these large gatherings of which I have spoken, although the mere giving is only a part-quite an important part, I grant, but only a part-of the ceremony of the potlatch as we understand it. At the same time, irrespective of the meaning of the word, the customs to which it is annexed are rooted in the social structure of the people, and these customs have tended to become in some measure depraved instead of becoming sublimed-in contact, that is, with our present type of civilization. The people themselves are now increasingly realizing that their responsibilities to one another, translated in terms of dollars and cents, are beggaring them beyond hope of recovery, and that the solace of the creditor Indian is poor indeed; for all he frequently obtains is the knowledge that the individual obligations of the many people to whom he has given gifts may some day be met, but that in the meantime all his security is the memory of the debtor supported by the age-old traditions of his people.
Of course, it can be easily understood that in largess there is the implication of a return of largess. Among the Indians this has been an inexorable condition. When the man or woman makes a gift in the potlatch there is the silent but otherwise entirely inescapable obligation to return the gift not less than twofold. When a blanket is given two blankets or their equivalent is the debt assumed for all time by the donee and his family. If the gift be made to a poor person, the debt then is more difficult to redeem; for often 250 per cent and even 300 per cent is required in settlement. Imagine the involutions of a custom where a poor man borrows at 250 per cent to potlatch a 200 per cent obligation.
But, as I have said, the giving of gifts is only one of the outward and visible ceremonies apparently indispensable to the gathering together of a large number of tribal members to whom will be advertised the changes in the tribal history of the person or persons drawing the people together. Nor is the giving indiscriminate. In its proper functioning there is an order of precedence as rigid and as impenetrable as that of any court or the list of the filtered drops from the distillation of the social elite. Then, also, each tribe has an order of precedence which has been established for all by their original spirits, or temenwos, in the progress of the creative birth of these people; as for example, in the definite case of the eagle tribe, which is highest in importance, the eagle bird itself is, or can be invested spiritually by any of the original spirits of the tribe; and in like manner at will departed from. And, be it understood, these spirits are not spirits of departing Indians or members of the eagle tribe of Indians, but they are the transcendent original spirits or temenwos, responsible for the investiture of human beings on earth with their own spiritual qualities. So it is with the wolf tribe; so it is with the bear tribe; so it is with all the other tribes.
Now that is a very highly-developed conception of creative conditions. Such a religious conviction of their creation is, to the Indian, as profoundly inspiring as is the Biblical story of creation to the Hebrew or the Christian. In such a background then, the incidents of birth, adolescence, marriage and death are sacredly sealed; it is with these incidents that the ceremonies are developing, and it is for these ceremonies that the potlatch of goods is both a card of invitation and an inducement to attend. The incidents of birth and death in Indian ceremonies have little enough which we can criticize, and I believe that the Indians in the Kwawkewlth agency are permitted to bury their dead according to their own rites. But the incident of marriage is entirely different. Girls in the tribe speaking the Kwawkala tongue are not married as we understand it. I am not now referring to the licensed marriage according to our laws or religion when I say that. These girls do not select their own husbands; they are not even sold by their parents; they are transferred to their husbands in perpetuity, shall I say, subject to the repayment of the mortgage by which they are held. In tradition, nothing, not even death, releases them from their biological mortgagee. Release can come only by repayment of the money received in the original

transaction. This physical bondage, of course, does not prevent the separation of so-called married people or the development of illegitimacy.
Let me enlarge on this so that the committee may understand completely and definitely the gravity of the situation. A certain man dies and leaves behind him a widow and one or two girls. To bury him and forget him the superior position he occupied in the tribe and among the phratries generally would be a crime against the traditions of the people, unthinkable to a true Indian, while the Indian wife herself would become definitely an outcast. There is no money, there is no property; none has been left by the deceased. There must be some declaration. Therefore there must be a potlatch. How can it be financed? The matter is settled by borrowing money for the potlatch, secured by mortgage on one or both of the girls. The girls, however, are only six and eight years old respectively. So, until they are ready for marriage, the mortgage over one or both may change hands several times. And neither the widowed mother nor the growing girls can know who the man will be who will claim the girls when their time comes.
Let me take another case. A chief has a son. It is time the boy was married. How fine it would be if the boy could one day be a Chief like his father! The chief looks around the various tribes and discovers a man with a daughter, who may be an idiot but is otherwise eligible because her father nas a copper, representing a potlatch value of some $5,000 or more. Negotiations are opened, and the girl's father agrees that he will permit the copper to become the property of the young couple by way of dowry with the girl, subject, however, to payment of the $5,000, paid as to a deposit of $200 on the sealing of the agreement, and a further $1,000 paid at the ceremony in reduction of the balance of the $5,000. The ceremony is held; the potlatch takes place; the mortgage money is paid over in part; the couple are mated, and thereafter day in and day out they-yes, they and all their friends and relatives-save and slave to complete the payment for the copper. It is easy to conceive the misery which will develop in the lives of that young couple, and to realize the truth that often the girl's body swells the fund which will make the copper their own sacred property.
The copper, let me explain, is the token coin, shall I say, of wealth among these Indians. It carries a varying and generally an accumulating value in the community; its possession is a hallmark of substance to its owner. It is handed down from generation to generation, or sold as a sacred asset. The

grudge against or the hatred of a man for his neighbour is in no way more maliciously and bitterly expressed than by the breaking of a copper and throwing the small fragments at the enemy, or, if he be dead, by nailing it over his coffin. Eternal woe follows the curse. Friends and relatives alike will struggle relentlessly to remove the burden.
Of course all this is not according to Canadian law, and is actually forbidden. But there is no policeman at Alert Bay, or at any of these ceremonies, and the Indian agent can do nothing. The Indians can fool the agent and the government, and they can fool the church too; for they will get married now in church and all will be well. And although the minister, the agent and the others know what has been done, the Christian ceremony proceeds and the Indian laughs as he dances, laughs as he potlatches, because in his clever, sly way he has fooled the white man. In 1935, just three years ago, three out of four girls trained for years in residental school in that area, on completing their term of scholarship went to their homes and were raped by their biological mortgagees, their Indian husbands. Well, some people will say, that is all right; that is their tradition, and that is their right to do things. But I charge all when I say that with knowledge alone comes responsibility. As we implant in these boys and girls our ideas of life and living, our codes of right and wrong, our whisperings of the romance of love and the selective choice of the loved one, we impose on them also the spiritual responsibility attaching inexorably to that knowledge, and we do not fail to attach it to ourselves. They live in the closely regulated atmosphere of school life and unconsciously develop their romances, and then, having learned enough of the viewpoint of their Canadian guardians, the government, they are dragged back into the worst feature of their native tradition and are lost to the finer ideals which we have struggled so hard to implant in their minds. True they often marry in church; but on both sides it is a hideous farce; for the minister too often senses if he does not know that the couple are thus seeking the religious cloak to cover their native susceptibilities.

Since 1917 the potlatch has been going on clandestinely, although the facts leak out before or after. While I was in Alert Bay many Indians of the surrounding tribes were gathered at Gilford island and Village island, and many from Kingcome

inlet had been there for weeks. They are bold now and are carrying on these practices consistently. The government is aware of these facts from its own agents as well as from many other sources, and it is essential that action be taken on that knowledge.
