Within the last day or two I have received a further letter from the Reverend F. Comley of Victoria, B.C., which is so related to what I am saying that I think it well to read it here. The letter is dated May 9, 1938:
Dear Mr. Taylor:
You will remember we had an exchange of opinions re the potlatch last year. You requested that if anything else arose in connection with the potlatch that I thought might be useful, would I send it along. During the past winter the Indians of the Kwawkewlth tribes have had a large gathering at Gwyas-dums. This is an Indian reserve on Gilford island about twenty-five miles from Alert Bay. It is isolated and the Indians have not used it very often during the past twenty-five years, but when I went to Alert Bay thirty years ago it was a popular winter resort for their winter dances, especially "the red fir dance." That should be "the red bark dance." They take the red bark, the fibrous matter under the outer bark, and colour it, bind it around their heads, arms and bodies, also a huge band around the neck. The principal character is the "Hamatsi." He is sent naked into the woods and comes out surrounded by a bodyguard, he is called "the wild man." I have seen this awful dance from beginning to end at Cape Mudge, Alert Bay, Village island and Kingcome inlet. It is one of the most ghastly spectacles I have ever seen. Everybody bitten by the "Hamatsi" must give a potlatch. It was forbidden years ago and seems to me very closely related to the famous sun dance of the prairie Indians. I have only seen it once during the last twelve years, but this year, gaining confidence by being left alone, the Indians returned to Gwyas-dums and ignored all law and order.
This is very bad for the Indians in every way as you know; children are neglected, nothing matters but this hideous dance goes on night and day. I brought this matter up in our provincial synod on Thursday, April 28th, and the following resolution was passed unanimously:
"Resolved

That this provincial synod of B.C. in session assembled unanimously endorse the action of Mr. J. S. Taylor, M.P. for the Nanaimo division of British Columbia in petitioning the government at Ottawa to have the present potlatch law enforced among the Kwawkewlth Indians of Vancouver Island and the adjoining islands and mainland."
Moved by Rev. F. Comley.
Seconded by Rev. H. C. R. Gibson.
The secretary should send this to you, but if he forgets you will know what we tried to do.
More power to your efforts is the desire of all real friends of the Indians.
With kind regards,
Very sincerely yours,
F. Comley.
In order that you may realize that this is a matter which I have taken up entirely apart from Rev. Mr. Comley, I may say that I have never met the gentleman, and have dealt with him entirely by correspondence.
P.S. I am saying not what someone has told me but what I saw as I lived with these people at Kingcome, Fort Rupert, Alert Bay, Cape Mudge, etc.
The reverend gentleman's letter leaves little room for doubt that a serious retrogression is sedulously developing among these people, and in order that the gravity of the situation might become patent to the hon. members of this committee I shall read from Stories of Early British Columbia by Doctor W. Wy-mond Walkem, published in 1914 in Vancouver. The late Doctor Walkem was the father of the present mayor of the city of Ladysmith, British Columbia, and the particular incident written about occurred in the fall of 1876. I read:-
For six weeks or more the "would-be" shaman wanders sadly through the mountains picking his sustenance from the berries, or edible tubers which everywhere abound. His nights were wholly consumed in the never-ending appeal to the temenwos, or to those spirits good or evil which may hear his distressing appeals for recognition. They are spiritualists, pure and simple, but their spiritualism differs from the modern "ism" of the present day, in that the spirit or "temenwos" whom they appeal to is in their belief an original spirit, and not the spirit of one who has died. Privation and lack of food no doubt reduce the Indian novitiate to a condition bordering on hysteria, and when in that condition he is liable to believe that he hears the answer to his plaintive wails for help and recognition. It is at this stage that he determines to return to the homes of his tribe. He is now dangerous-a species of demon, whose hunger must be appeased by flesh.
Slowly and stealthily he makes his way back to where his former companions are anxiously awaiting his return. When within a short distance of his place of birth, he rushes in with frightful yells, and woe betide the unfortunate native whom he first encouters on his way. He leaps upon him like a wild beast, and probably bites a piece out of his victim's arm. No resistance is offered, as it is considered a great privilege to be thus bitten by the future shaman. The man is famished and he devours the piece of flesh like a hungry dog. If, instead of meeting with one of his owti kind, he sees a dog, he will, if possible, seize it with both hands and rend the animal in pieces.
Once inside the village or settlement, four or more sturdy members of the tribe pounce on him and confine him for the last and trying ordeal which I saw in the case of Johnny Chiceete, or "grey-haired" Johnny, as he v'as known to the whites. I will describe this shortly.
Then I turn to it:-
About three-quarters of an hour had elapsed when the drummers in the centre of the ground space began to beat a regular rhythmic strcke upon the gigantic drums which they had before

them. Four shamans were walking up and down in this space, one of whom reminded me of a huge baboon I had seen at the zoological gardens in Regent's Park. While singing they were shaking rattles, as well as their ankles, most assiduously, which were adorned with shells and small rattles. In a few moments some of the women and men stepped out upon the floor, and began to move about in the usual dancing step. Their tunes are always the same, and the movements of the dancers also. These dances were kept up for some time, one middle-aged man showed his gastric capacity by Bwallowing a square gin bottle of dog fish oil without drawing a breath. He subsided in a helpless condition upon the earthen floor, from which he was promptly packed off to one of the platform seats.
At 8 o'clock everything was perfectly quiet, so quiet indeed, that you could have heard a pin drop in the dusty floor. Then a noise, with much howling was suddenly heard proceeding from the roof. In a few moments a human body was pushed through the square hole in the roof of the rancherie. As the body dangled inside of the skylight, as I will call it, I was able to see that the figure was pendant by four hooks and chains, from the pulley I have already mentioned as being at the ends of the four poles, lying across the skylight. It was the body of Johnny Chiceete which was dangling in the upper air. He was hanging suspended by four hooks, one through the muscles of each upper arm, and one through the muscles of each thigh. He was completely naked with the exception of a loin covering made from the inner bark of the cedar.
His attendants on the roof lowered him slowly to the ground, then back to the roof and down again. This was repeated three times. While going up and down he shouted out some words which I took to be a specie of ritual, for at every pause in his speech he was answered by the shamans on the ground below. They kept walking up and down in line for about twenty feet and back, silent while Johnny Chiceete was speaking, and picking up the words just as Johnny ceased. No sign on Johnny's face told of the horrible torture he must have been enduring. He could not have been more quiet if he had been lowered and raised in a capacious basket.
At the termination of the third drop, four big powerful members of his tribe rushed out and grasped him by the arms, while the hooks were kept quite taut to prevent his breaking away. Straps were slipped round his arms to give his captors a good firm hold and command of his body. The hooks were then removed, and Johnny sprang to his feet, and attempted to break away.
Many of the audience, fearful he should escape from his captors, began to seek safer positions. Now came the most curious part of the ceremony. Ten Indians came down the circular pathway, naked to the waist. Johnny saw them, and began to gnash his teeth in anticipation of a feast, for he was fearfully hungry, having arrived from the mountains a short hour before his appearance on the roof. As Johnny strained like a dog on the leash to get at the first semi-naked Siwash, he seemed more like a wild beast than a human being.
Gradually he dragged his keepers to his first victim, the shamans following in the rear with pieces or strips of cotton and Indian balm.

Arriving at the first man, he seized his arm, and bit a large piece out of it, and then passed on towards the next. The shamans to our surprise called our special attention to the wound in the first man's arm, to show there was no fake about it, I suppose. Then they applied some balm or ointment, and wrapped up the whole in cotton.
After binding up the wound on the first man's arm, a shaman slipped a ten-dollar geld piece into the victim's hand, according, as I was afterwards told by Mr. Horne, to an arrangement between the victim and Johnny Chiceete's friends. After his first performance with his teeth, Mrs. Horne and Mrs. Grant retired from the building. It was too horrible for their sensitive nerves. Mr. Horne, Mr. Grant and I stayed on to see the ceremony through. Johnny completed his round with the hired victims, and just as he finished with the last, he saw a small dog near the platform, which he seized with both hands and began to eat alive. He was pushed, with the dog in his hands, towards the entrance and was taken by his friends to a cabin specially prepared for him, where his hook wounds received special attention. All of those who supplied Johnny with arms to bite were rewarded in the same way as the first one was, who by the way was an Indian known to the whites as Siwash George. I only heard the names of three others. They were Three Fingered Jimmy, Saweetlum and Potato Johnny.
To face this matter, officially it must be regretted that there are no policemen at Alert Bay. I do not refer to the provincial police. Fine men they are, but they cannot deal in a proper manner with this which is a purely federal and departmental matter. The government should most certainly have a policeman and police engineer with a suitable fast boat to cope with the situation as it now exists. This boat and these officers should be based on Alert Bay.
But this action will noit in itself be sufficient. I consider that the chiefs who persist in potlatching and intriguing in the more uncivilized customs and traditions of their people should be denied recognition in every sense as chiefs by this government. They should be deposed officially by the government from their chieftainship. Further, some element of discrimination should be developed by the government which would distinguish the prac-tiser of the potlatch from the Indian, Christian or other, who has definitely renounced it.
We are perpetuating a serious evil and senselessly throwing away much money now being expended if we do nothing more than teach the Indian to despise our guidance. In effect, some of these people are in real danger of becoming more certainly savages than they now may be. These matters all want close investigation and a thorough airing. It is evidently not for nothing that the Indians at Kingcome inlet have taken to exchanging IOU's in their potlatches. In

addition to what I have said I am prevented by time-not inclination-from reading letters of unequivocal value from men of long residence among these tribes, and I would certainly have liked to mention the opinions of students of Indian tradition and lore like Professor Hill Tout and many others. This I will say, however, that whatever has to be done-and it is important to record it and accept it thus-must be done firmly, considerately, intelligently, so that the Indians themselves may preserve the sublimed values of their customs, while casting away the practices to which they have been slaves.
I have claimed that contact with civilization tends to bring this about naturally if the contact is made real and forceful. There was a time in Europe when we stuck the skulls of our enemies on spears or poles in front of our tents or lodges. To-day we raise stone gate-posts and carve round balls on top to remind us of those early days. At one time before we understood the constructional technique of foundations we, the white people, offered living sacrifices, to seal the cracks in our city walls, our great buildings, our cathedrals. The good book tells us that Jericho's walls were rebuilt in the sacrifice of the first-born of the builder and they were completed in the sacrifice of the builder himself.

speechtext: I must inform the hon. member that he has exhausted the time at his disposal.
I would crave the indulgence of the committee for another few moments.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure we would like to hear the remainder of this instructive statement on potlatching. Now that I have made my little contribution, perhaps the hon. member could continue.

I thank the right hon. gentleman. Hamburg's city walls contained the bones of many sacrificed as votive appeasement of the wrath of the gods. These elementary conceptions gave way in the face of civilization and Christianity until in the cracks in churches lighted candles symbolized the offering of a life and were walled up in the necessary repair.
Everywhere this sublimation goes on and knowledge breeds its kind, but we do wrong to ourselves and the Indian if we complacently regard his efforts towards civilization as struggles for which we are in no wise responsible. I do most earnestly urge the minister to believe that the complaints of many citizens
who are deeply interested in these promising and lovable people are real and prompted by the most worthy ideals.
I understand that the minister has also been very fully advised by the Indian agent on the spot. Surely his understanding, training, and devotion to the service should also be set on the scales in this matter. It is possible that some advantage might develop from civil marriages to avoid the present farcical practices. Marriages could later be solemnized for Christian members of Christian churches, but do not let us perpetuate this evil of the potlatch, as it is now being perpetuated.

As I represent the district in which these horrible orgies are supposed to have taken place, it is perhaps my duty to say something in defence of these poor Indians whose character and reputation have been so bitterly and unfairly assailed. I yield to no one in this house in my regard for the good qualities of heart and mind of the hon. member for Nanaimo, but his judgment is negligible; that is the trouble.
I have listened with amused horror to his remarks which contained a little bit of sordid truth, very much exaggerated, and an immensity of imagination which would make another volume of Grimm's fairy tales. The two mixed together have produced the treatise which the hon. member has read. These people live from 200 to 250 miles away from the district which the hon. gentleman represents. They are in the far northern part of the district I represent.
In some respects we are a peculiar people in Comox-AIbemi, in a scriptural sense, and we do not very much care for outside interference. We somehow think we are capable of looking after our own political affairs, and we believe in doing as we would be done by. Six months ago I was asked to go down to the district represented by the hon. member and to interfere in a matter connected with the Indians. But it was purely a local trouble, one which had nothing to do with my district; and as it had nothing to do with provincial rights or interests I declined. I recommended that they go to the hon. member who I said I knew was a man of good intention and of good heart, and one who would do what he could. I w'as doing only as I would be done by. Therefore we hesitate to be guided by the advice of the hon. member.
So far as his statements are concerned, he has been talking out of the dead past. Let us realize that the passage of the Indian from savagery to civilization has been one which has taken place in two generations. In the case of the white man, it has been ten centuries. He is trying to compare the one with
Supply-Indian Affairs

the other. If we are going to do that, we shall have to go back to the days when maidens were sacrificed on the altars of the Druids. That has long since passed. It is only two generations since the Indians were living under the same conditions as we were so long ago.
I can illustrate what happened to my hon. friend. I know quite well what occurred. He went up there looking for horrors, and he got them. Let me give an illustration of a similar case. Many years ago when I was Indian agent there came into my office a gentleman bearing credentials from the Ottawa department. They instructed me that he had come to write up Indian folklore and I was to give him every assistance possible. A Mr. Cox was chief of the white police at that time and he could talk the Indian language. I enlisted his sympathies, and we arranged for this gentleman to talk with some of the old people. In each band or tribe there is generally one old person who is regarded more or less as the historian of the band. He gets up at potlatch time and hands on the traditions of the tribe. That is the only way they can do it. I arranged for this gentleman to get in touch with the historian of this tribe, but we found out that that was not satisfactory. That would involve sitting in a dirty Indian hut with a mud floor and possibly in unclean conditions, draughty, smelly and everything else. He did not like that.
In the course of a few days he intimated to us that he was able to run things in his own way. He got hold of an Indian boy just out of school. He paid him what was a fabulous sum in those days, S3 a day, to come down and sit in the comfortable hotel room and furnish him with this folklore. Presently it got noised about what wonderful folklore this gentleman was getting. This information came to Mr. Cox and myself and we hunted up this Indian boy. We knew very well that the stuff he was giving this gentleman was pure nonsense. We knew it had no relation whatever to the folklore as we knew it. We asked this Indian lad what he meant by fooling this gentleman from Ottawa. The result was that we learned that this boy had given him what little folklore he knew, and then finished off with a garbled version of what he had gotten from a book in the Indian school. I often yearned to see that book published. This boy had a very comfortable job, and he wanted to keep it. The man from Ottawa wanted to get some folklore under comfortable circumstances, and he got it.
My hon. friend went snooping around in a district 250 miles away from the country with which he was familiar. He was asking for

horrors and he got them. He mentioned this Mr. Comley. Mr. Comley is quite an old gentleman, a former church missionary. He referred to this horrible red bark dance at a place called Quathiaski Cove.
I never mentioned that.

In the early days.

That is right. I hold in my hand a letter which appeared in the public press, from the Reverend M. F. Eby, a very reliable man whom I know well. He is in charge of the missionary society at this place called Cape Mudge, and he writes to protest strongly against Mr. Comley having suggested that this dance had been held by his Indians. He states that they are quite decent Indians and have not practised that dance for many years.
That is precisely what the Reverend Mr. Comley said.

Mr. Comley writes back to
Mr. Eby, and he prints the letter. Mr. Comley blames the press and states that he was misunderstood, that it did not take place recently at Cape Mudge, but twenty-nine years ago. He describes it as "The Most Devilish Spectacle" he has ever seen. Then he goes on to elaborate upon the whole thing. Remember, this is Mr. Comley, not me. It is interesting to note that the words "The Most Devilish Spectacle," are in capitals. He describes how this awful dance is carried on and states that the children are neglected. Are not our white children sometimes neglected when their parents go out to play bridge? He states these dances cause strife and malice, but unfortunately to-day we find strife and malice not only between people but among nations. But this "devilish spectacle" took place twenty-nine years ago. That is a long time ago.
Then he talks about selling women. He has twisted a very small matter and tried to make it into a large one. We do not need to go so far back into history to the time when the chiefs of the Scottish clans or the knights in England had the bestowal of the wards under their authority. Quite often a girl was given to one of the knights, and if the gentleman was a seemly looking man, the girl was not long in accepting him. That is the true explanation of this selling. There is absolutely no justification for the statement that these girls are biologically raped by their

Supply-Indian Affairs
husbands. As to the tale that there is a mortgage which is in effect until it is repaid, it is like our dowry. The trouble I had when I was Indian agent was in getting the men and women to stick together. Wives and husbands had a playful habit of getting rid of each other and taking newer and younger mates. It was not a case of getting back their mortgage money. All the time I was Indian agent I never heard of one woman being sold in that way.
Another complaint is that there is no policeman at Alert Bay, and then he qualifies that statement later on by saying he meant no dominion policeman. By making such a statement he insults the reputation of the provincial police, a very fine body of men. I wrote to the chief of police in Victoria asking him if he had any trouble in handling the crime situation at Alert Bay. He told me that he had not. He said they had two men there now and if an extra one was needed, he would be put on. He told me that there was no need for an extra man up to the present. Then I asked him about these dreadful orgies that were supposed to go on and this potlatch business. It turned out that this was a most trivial matter. He told me there had not been a murder, a bank robbery or a burglary in many years. The worst crime was drunkenness and he told me he averaged one and a half cases a week over a period of two years. The provincial police are perfectly capable of handling the Indians. They also administer other dominion statutes, because that is part of the bargain made between the dominion and the province.
A long quotation was made from a book written by Mr. Walkem, describing conditions in 1876, sixty-two years ago. He talked about eating dogs. There used to be something about taking bites out of a living dog, but that never occurred in the district about which he is talking. That was away up in the north, and that practice has been out of date for at least thirty or forty years. He has been loaded up with all this stuff of the past. He wants to know why the law is not enforced. The law is strictly enforced. Any one who takes part in any Indian festival, dance or other ceremony of which the giving away or giving back of money, goods or articles of any sort forms a part, is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months and not less than two months. The question is whether it is wise to take these Indians by the throat, so to speak, and try to make Christians out of them. Here is a telegram
I received from the Indians. They did not send it collect either, as many white men would. It reads:
Investigator on potlatch went Alert Bay only, which not fair deal. We want investigator for both Indians and Indian agent, not one-sided. Hold his report until you hear from us. We desire square deal and want honest and truthful man. We know he is taking report on potlatch which he got from young people, not from older people.
And they send a letter in which they say the same thing. It is not in very good English, but they say that they are not satisfied with the work of the investigator who was at Alert Bay-that is, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor)-and they want an investigator to interview them and their officials. The letter went on to say that there were people who were deadly against their custom who would feature one instance, possibly an undesirable one, and ignore everything else in its favour, and also listen to gossip and rumour.
I wrote to the minister and asked if he knew anything about the matter in his department, and I have a reply saying that he did not sanction anybody going up there and that he knew nothing about it.
I have a further letter from the chiefs to say that they had word that a Mr. Taylor was at Alert Bay, who is also an M.P.- that is how they express it-they ask me to find out what knowledge of the potlatch Mr. Taylor got from the people, and they remark with a good deal of truth that what he should have done was to meet the chiefs and the people of this agency. As a matter of fact, he was trespassing and stirring up one bunch of Indians against another, which is illegal.
There is one other phase. My hon. friend quoted the good book. Let me follow his example. Scripture says something about taking the beam out of your own eye before you meddle with the mote in your brother's eye. And when he was pussyfooting around my district, without invitation, and with a very restricted welcome, what was going on in his own district? I have a cutting here from a paper published in Nanaimo, the capital of his seat, with a population of about nine thousand people, and eight hundred Indians were turned loose there one day, these dreadful debauches, in his own capital cityl Here is the heading on the article describing it: "Day long potlatch is held at Nanaimo." The article goes on to say that eight hundred Indians participated and it reveals the dark and awesome tale. It all amounts to this: There was a marriage, which
Supply-Indian Affairs

is neither an illegal nor an uncommon thing, and they had a feast, also not unusual. The article also goes on to say:
Potlatches are banned under British Columbia law, but special sanction was obtained for the Nanaimo celebration.
Very well, it was illegal, but special sanction was obtained. When or where? Was the hon. member a party to it? If he was, then he was allowing a potlatch to go on in his own district while he was denouncing one in mine. If he was not a party to it he was neglecting his duty by not taking the beam out of his own eye. It would have been very much better if he had attended, to put it roughly, to the details of his own district.
But I must hurry on. I have here a letter from these people. They write requesting me to get in touch with His Excellency the Governor General to ask if he would act as patron of the opening of their new church, to be dedicated by the bishop, and the ceremony in connection with a totem pole which they had erected at great cost and trouble to the memory of King George. I have the very kindly letter of his excellency saying that he was pleased to be a patron and that he was reporting their action of loyalty to the king. Then I have an invitation, very nicely printed, with "God Save the King" on it in dialect, and a picture of the totem pole. I will send the two photographs over to the minister and the Prime Minister, but they are to be passed as an order for return because I want them back again. I have here the Victoria Colonist, a half page of which is devoted to the ceremony. There is a picture of the hall and of the church, a much better one than I worship in at home; the bishop is shown in his robes on the steps of the church, and there is a picture of the communicants taking their first communion. It is very nicely written up, and there is also a picture of the totem pole. These are hardly the people, one would think, who would indulge in these bloody orgies about which my hon. friend talks. Surely good progress has been made in two generations.
Let me cite South Africa. They just recently, within the last few months, passed a law allowing native courts to be set up to deal with the natives in accordance with native law and customs, and among other things polygamy is allowed, which will horrify my hon. friend. The idea is to make decent, Christian natives out of these people, instead of imitation white men. They have passed that law in Africa, declaring that the law shall be in

accordance with the native customs, and that is how to make these people Christians, not by force of arms and by policemen, but by teaching them in a reasonable way.
Here is what a man, a missionary, wrote to the paper the other day; I quote one paragraph:
The mistake we have been making is in trying to make of the Indian what he was never intended to be-a white man. The church, by adopting compulsory measures, may succeed in suppressing the potlatch but she will never win the Indian.
He will respond, as he has always done, to sound leadership, wise counsel and, above all, consistent example.
It goes on to say:
It is not the intention of this letter to minimize the evils in some of these old Indian customs-
Nor am I trying to do it.
-or to cast any reflection upon those who, under great handicaps, are labouring in Indian communities: its object is respectfully to commend to the leaders of the church a far better and more effective way of dealing with this problem, namely the Christian way of sympathetic understanding and moral suasion.
Which is the better method? The policeman with his revolver in his hand saying, you shall not do that, or the kindly moral suasion of the church, leading the Indian step by step? My hon. friend himself says there has not been a public potlatch since 1916. The custom is wearing itself out. It only needs time and moderation. It is the old principle again, if you tell a man not to do something that he has been habituated to doing for a hundred years, that never stops him; but if you tell him that it is not a good thing, you can gradually lead him to different ideals. That is better than putting a policeman there and trying to make the Indians what they were never intended to be-white men.
